body: The transformer shortage is turning into a capacity glut on the margin line before the revenue line. Watch OPM, not order books. The value in this theme today is in **transmission EPC and towers** (Skipper, Transrail), at 14–24x with 1.8–1.9x order cover. Pure data-centre exposure in small caps is either priced (Marine, KRN, QPOWER at 55–83x) or not yet showing up in earnings (Techno).

- The case shows the structure of the edge. JS lost money in cash and futures, which acted as the "lever", and made it back many times over in options, which were the "payload". The asymmetry depends on scale: only a firm with balance sheet large enough to move index constituents can do it. Retail option buyers on expiry day were the likely counterparties in aggregate.
- Whatever SEBI finally rules, the economics are clear. A few global firms extracted billions of dollars a year from India's weekly-expiry options market. That is consistent with the SEBI category data in section 2.

**Same playbook, opposite outcome (leverage and concentration)**
- Archegos / Bill Hwang: the fund managed about $36bn of capital, but derivatives gave it about $160bn of stock exposure. Its 2021 collapse cost banks more than $10bn. Hwang was sentenced to 18 years on 20 Nov 2024 and ordered to pay more than $9bn in restitution. — [DOJ SDNY](https://www.justice.gov/usao-sdny/pr/founder-and-head-archegos-capital-management-bill-hwang-sentenced-18-years-prison); [Al Jazeera](https://www.aljazeera.com/economy/2024/11/20/archegoss-bill-hwang-sentenced-to-18-years-in-prison-for-massive-us-fraud). **MYTH CHECK:** the often-quoted "$20bn" loss figure is not supported. Reported bank losses are about $10bn.
- LTCM (1998): Nobel laureates Merton and Scholes were on its board. It lost about $4.6bn in under four months, with about $4.7bn of equity against more than $124.5bn of borrowings (over 25:1 debt-to-equity at the start of 1998). Some sources give 20:1, or about 200:1 at the peak, using different measures. — [Wikipedia: LTCM](https://Www.Wikipedia.org/wiki/LTCM); [McGraw-Hill case](https://highered.mheducation.com/sites/dl/free/0077151569/977786/c26i_LTCM.pdf); [Fortune 1998](https://money.cnn.com/magazines/fortune/fortune_archive/1998/10/26/250015/index.htm)
- Buffett on LTCM: "To make money they didn't have and didn't need, they risked what they did have and did need… That is just plain foolish." It is usually attributed to his 1998 University of Florida talk. The wording varies between sources, and I did not verify it against the transcript. — [Novel Investor](https://novelinvestor.com/buffetts-lessons-long-term-capital-management/); [Marginal Revolution](https://marginalrevolution.com/marginalrevolution/2007/04/buffett_on_ltcm.html)
- Harshad Mehta (1992): used fake bank receipts to channel bank money into equities. One estimate says over ₹40,000 crore of market wealth was erased in the crash. SEBI was given statutory power in 1992 in the aftermath. — [Samco](https://www.samco.in/knowledge-center/articles/3-stock-market-scams-that-shook-the-nation/); [Upstox](https://upstox.com/learning-center/share-market/history-of-stock-market-crashes-in-india) (aggregators, so these are lower-quality sources)
- Ketan Parekh (1999–2001): circular trading and pump-and-dump in the "K-10" stocks, arrested by the CBI in 2001, convicted in 2008. — [Wikipedia: Ketan Parekh](https://en.wikipedia.com/wiki/Ketan_Parekh); [iPleaders](https://blog.ipleaders.in/ketan-parekh-scam/)
- Indian small caps: the BSE Smallcap fell about 68% in 2008. The Nifty Smallcap 100's maximum fall that year was about 76%. — [Business Standard](https://business-standard.com/article/markets/is-the-worst-over-for-small-caps-here-s-what-past-data-indicates-118120900518_1.html); [5paisa](https://www.5paisa.com/blog/small-cap-index-30-percent-below-peak-36-percent-trading-days). In 2018 the BSE Smallcap fell about 28% from its January peak to September and 23.5% over the calendar year. 67 index stocks were already down more than 50% by June, and 111 stocks were down more than 50% by late June. — [Business Standard (67 stocks)](https://www.business-standard.com/article/markets/67-stocks-from-bse-smallcap-index-fall-more-than-50-in-2018-118060500249_1.html); [Business Standard (111 stocks)](https://business-standard.com/amp/article/markets/bse-smallcap-index-hits-9-month-low-111-stocks-tank-over-50-in-cy18-118062800350_1.html); [BS year-end](https://www.business-standard.com/article/pti-stories/small-stocks-lose-sheen-tumbles-nearly-24-in-2018-118123100707_1.html). From 2004 onwards, the small-cap index spent 36% of trading days more than 30% below its peak. — [5paisa](https://www.5paisa.com/blog/small-cap-index-30-percent-below-peak-36-percent-trading-days)
- Indian retail derivatives:
  - SEBI study, FY22–FY24: more than 93% of over 1 crore individual F&O traders lost money, an average loss of about ₹2 lakh each. — [Tribune](https://www.tribuneindia.com/news/business/93-retail-traders-lost-money-in-fo-in-3-years-sebi-study/amp)
  - FY25: about 91% lost money, with net losses of ₹1,05,603 crore (vs ₹74,812 crore in FY24). — [Business Standard](https://www.business-standard.com/amp/markets/news/net-losses-of-traders-in-fo-widens-in-fy25-sebi-study-125070701221_1.html); [Value Research](https://www.valueresearchonline.com/stories/225398/average-trader-lost-rs-1-1-lakh-fo-fy25/)
  - FY26 study: 87.7% still lost. Loss rates fall with the size of a trader's equity holdings, from 93% for those with no equity holdings to 58% for those holding more than ₹10 crore. — [CorpLaw Updates](https://www.corplawupdates.in/updates/sebi-equity-derivatives-retail-trader-study-fy26)

`case_study:future-group-2020` | 2022-07-20 | tickers: FRETAIL, FEL, FLFL | confidence: verified

Kishore Biyani's Future Group (Big Bazaar) grew via debt-funded store expansion, frequent restructurings and demergers. Future Retail peaked ~Rs 550-600 in 2018 (unverified exact) and fell to ~Rs 2-5 by 2022 (~-99%). Promoters' FRL stake fell from 47% (Dec 2019) to ~14% (Mar 2022) as pledged shares were invoked. Covid lockdowns (2020) tipped an over-levered group (group debt reported ~Rs 25,000-30,000 cr); a Rs 24,713 cr asset sale to Reliance (Aug 2020) was blocked by Amazon's arbitration (Amazon had bought 49% of Future Coupons in 2019) and then rejected by secured lenders in Apr 2022 after Reliance took over 900+ stores. FRL was admitted to insolvency in Jul 2022, Future Enterprises later. Visible flags: (1) negative free cash flow for a decade; growth funded by debt and asset sales; (2) promoter pledges consistently high; (3) repeated group reorganisations, cross-holdings and related-party leases making cash flows hard to follow; (4) low ROCE vs D-Mart's debt-free owned-store model; (5) the Amazon deal itself was a pledge-relief transaction. Lesson: compare business models: D-Mart (owned stores, no debt, EDLP) compounded while Future (leased, levered, promoter-pledged) collapsed in the same market. FCF negative + pledges + restructurings = disqualifier.

**Lesson:** Leverage + pledges in thin-margin retail = fragile
**Spotted early by:** credit analysts; comparison with DMART
**Links:** illustrates -> `insight:promoter-pledge-group-contagion`, illustrates -> `insight:disqualifiers`, illustrates -> `insight:value-trap-patterns`

`insight:altman-z-score` | 2026-11-19 | tickers: - | confidence: single-source

Altman (1968) manufacturing model: Z = 1.2*(WC/TA) + 1.4*(RE/TA) + 3.3*(EBIT/TA) + 0.6*(Mkt cap/Total liabilities) + 1.0*(Sales/TA). Zones: Z > 2.99 safe; 1.81-2.99 grey; < 1.81 distress (some tables use 1.8/3.0). Z' (private firms, book equity) cut-offs ~1.23/2.90. Z'' (non-manufacturers/emerging markets, drops sales/TA): Z'' = 6.56*X1 + 3.26*X2 + 6.72*X3 + 1.05*X4, distress < 1.1, safe > 2.6 (EM version adds +3.25 constant). Altman's original sample classified ~95% of bankrupts correctly one year ahead, with accuracy falling sharply 2+ years out -- it's a near-term distress gauge, not a fraud detector. Indian use: run on consolidated numbers; exclude banks/NBFCs/insurers (use leverage, ALM, divergence instead); market-value term (X4) can mask distress in bubbles (Adani 2022, Nikola) -- check with book-equity Z'. Low Z examples pre-collapse: Jet Airways (negative RE and WC), Kingfisher, Future Retail, Unitech 2008. A low Z with rising pledges or CP dependence is a disqualifier; a low Z in a cyclical at trough can be a turnaround -- require debt reduction evidence.

**Links:** part_of -> `insight:forensic-redflag-checklist`, about -> `insight:avoid-ruin`
**Sources:** <https://www.gurufocus.com/term/mscore> ; <https://developers.lseg.com/en/article-catalog/article/analysing-sp500-companies-stocks-with-beneish-m-score-and-altman-z-score> ; <https://piyushgupta344.github.io/fin-ratios/ratios/composite>

`case_study:palantir-2022-2026` · tickers US-PLTR · confidence: verified

Direct listing Sept 2020 (~$10). Low ~$6 in late 2022 (all-time low $6.55 by May 2022; ~$5.9 Dec 2022), -87% from the Jan 2021 meme peak (~$45) [peak unverified]. P/S fell from 35x (Sep 2021) to 8.5x (Sep 2022). Then: first GAAP profit Q4 2022 and consecutive profitable quarters (S&P 500 entry Sept 2024); AIP launched 2023 with 'bootcamps' (560 done by Feb 2024) that accelerated US commercial deals; Q1 2026 revenue +85% y/y to $1.633bn. Peak ~$207 (Nov 2025) [unverified] ≈ 35x from the low. P/S hit 137x (Aug 2025, Motley Fool) — the stock outran even 85% growth. Split: overwhelmingly rerating (P/S 8.5x -> 137x ≈ 16x) vs revenue ~2.5x. By Nov 13 2026: ~-36% from ATH, ~60x sales, forward P/E ~85 vs ~200 at peak — multiple compression despite growth. EARLY SIGNAL visible 2023: sustained GAAP profitability (index eligibility), accelerating US commercial customer count and deal size after bootcamps, rule-of-40 score rising, while the stock was at ~8x sales. Who caught it: retail community, Wedbush's Dan Ives, ARK (bought 2022-23) [unverified]. LESSON: real fundamental acceleration started it, but a 16x multiple expansion means future returns depend on keeping hype; Motley Fool notes only 7 other software firms ever traded >100x sales and all fell >=70% from peak valuation.

- **Start → end:** ~$6 (2022 low) → ~$207 peak (Nov 2025) [unverified]; ~-36% by Nov 2026 (~35x peak)
- **EPS vs rerating:** ~16x P/S rerating vs ~2.5x revenue
- **Max drawdown:** -87% (2021-22); -36% (2025-26)
- **Early signal:** GAAP profitability -> S&P eligibility; AIP bootcamps; US commercial acceleration at 8x sales
- **Who caught it:** retail, Dan Ives, ARK [unverified]
- **Ended/stalled:** multiple compression from late 2025
- **Lesson:** >100x sales base rate is brutal even with 85% growth

`strategy:munger-inversion` | confidence: **single-source** | tags: global, process, behavior, quality

Core practices: (1) Inversion - before buying, list how the investment could fail (pre-mortem) and avoid those paths; 'all I want to know is where I'm going to die, so I'll never go there.' (2) Latticework - check a thesis with models from several disciplines: incentives, scale economics, network effects, compounding, opportunity cost, regression to the mean. (3) A bias checklist from 'The Psychology of Human Misjudgment' (1995): incentive-caused bias, social proof, commitment/consistency, deprival super-reaction, envy, denial, authority, and 'lollapalooza' when several combine (e.g., Indian IPO/SME manias). (4) Few great bets, held long; 'the big money is not in the buying and selling but in the waiting.' (5) Quality over cheapness: wonderful business at a fair price. Evidence: Munger's own partnership showed -30%+ years in 1973-74, so concentration requires capacity to endure drawdowns. Individual use: a written one-page pre-mortem and bias check per stock.

`strategy:andrade-capital-cycle` | confidence: **single-source** | tags: india, process, contrarian, cyclical

Look at supply, not demand. (1) Find industries where capacity growth has stalled - years of poor returns, no new projects, weak players exiting or being acquired. (2) Own the survivors with the best cost position and balance sheet ('last man standing'); as demand catches up with frozen supply, utilisation and pricing rise and margins expand sharply. (3) Prefer high asset-turnover, capital-light models where incremental growth needs little capex. (4) Exit when the industry starts announcing big capacity additions or new entrants rush in. Indicators for Indian investors: capacity utilisation data (cement, steel, paper), industry capex announcements, consolidation deals, number of listed players and their losses, P/B near cycle lows. Related evidence: the Indian capital goods index took ~2007-2021 to regain its peak after a capacity boom - the inverse of this strategy. Risk: demand may never return (structural decline).

Links: person:kenneth-andrade (about); case_study:capital-goods-2007 (about)

Sources: <https://www.flame.edu.in/academics/flame-investment-lab/resources/kenneth-andrade>

2. Every number checked against two sources.

body:
- **Valuation timing matters.** Since 2004, every negative 5-year Nifty return started at P/E ≥ 24.5;
  starting below P/E 12 gave ~29%/yr.
- **Indian winners mostly grew profits;** only ~37% of the median gain came from a higher P/E. Stocks
  that ended their run at P/E 70+ are mostly lower today (median −48%).
- **Small caps fall >20% about every 2 years** and spent 36% of days (2004–26) >30% below their peak.
- **Tone isn't an edge in India** — optimistic concall language moves prices short-term but doesn't
  predict results. Checking promises vs delivery is the edge.
- **Never trust a company's own "no pledge" statement** — check the exchange data.
